idiom_name: try/except with a cached substitute (contextlib.suppress for ignorable failures)
implementation_notes: Python expresses degradation as ordinary exception handling: wrap the primary in try/except for the dependency's exception types, substitute (cache lookup, default value, empty collection) and mark the result. contextlib.suppress is the narrow form for failures that are genuinely ignorable, and asyncio.timeout bounds the attempt so the fallback runs before the request deadline. The classic degraded-mode object collapses into the returned value plus one recorder (logger/metric); keep a policy object only when several dependencies share the same ladder, otherwise the branch stays next to the call it protects.
pitfalls: A bare except (or a broad except Exception) turns bugs and misconfiguration into "degraded service"; asyncio's CancelledError is a BaseException precisely so cancellation is not swallowed, and neither should genuine defects be.
Mutable module-level caches shared by all requests and tenants can serve one tenant's stale data to another; scope the fallback store per request or per tenant.
contextlib.suppress without a log or metric makes the degradation permanent and invisible - suppress only errors whose absence you can prove is harmless.
